body.text: India's carbon market cannot offset CBAM on its own, but a mix of export diversification, transition finance, and EU cooperation could turn the mechanism into a lever for industrial decarbonisation
Image Source: Getty Images

In January 2026, India and the European Union (EU) delivered a geopolitical game-changer by concluding negotiations on a free trade agreement (FTA) and ending a nearly two-decade deadlock. Together, they account for 25 percent of global GDP and nearly one-third of international trade, and both are keen to deepen their economic ties as a strategic firewall against intensifying great-power rivalry. While the FTA dramatically improves India’s market access to Europe, the contentious Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) simultaneously raises the carbon-adjusted cost of accessing that market. The central question, therefore, is whether India’s emerging carbon market can convert this apparent trade-climate conflict into a lever for industrial decarbonisation.

India’s exposure to CBAM is substantial, given its dependence on highly emissions-intensive sectors such as iron, steel, aluminium, fertilisers, and cement. In 2023 (the most recent year for which consistent data are available), India's CBAM-affected exports were valued at roughly US$6.4 billion, with iron and steel alone contributing US$5.41 billion, followed by aluminium at US$0.97 billion, cement at US$5.9 million, and fertilisers at US$2 million. In practice, since January 2026, EU importers of Indian steel, aluminium, or fertilisers have been liable to bear an additional carbon cost by purchasing CBAM certificates, priced in line with the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) carbon price — around EUR 75 per tonne of CO₂ equivalent as of March 2026.

The EU is India’s third-largest trading partner, with trade in goods worth EUR 118 billion in 2025, accounting for 11.1 percent of India’s total trade. Indeed, the initial effects of CBAM are already evident in India’s iron and steel exports to the EU. As of April 2026, these exports had declined by 13 percent since the CBAM rollout in January 2026.

Highly emissions-intensive and deeply integrated into global value chains, the iron and steel sector accounts for 60 percent or more of India’s total CBAM-embedded emissions exposure to the EU. India, one of the leading suppliers of iron and steel to the EU, also ranks among the highest globally in the direct emissions intensity of steel production, at 4.68 tCO₂/t. This is roughly twice the EU27 average of 2.3 tCO₂/t for a comparable product mix (Figure 1).
Note: The figure shows unweighted average emissions intensities (tonnes of CO₂e per tonne of product) for all iron and steel product codes.

India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), a government-run scheme, serves a dual purpose: establishing a legal basis for India's carbon markets and meeting the climate targets pledged in its Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) under the Paris Agreement. Adopted in 2022 through an amendment to the Energy Conservation Act, 2001, the CCTS aims to cover emissions along domestic value chains and issues carbon credit certificates (CCCs) for emissions reductions.
This architectural mismatch between India's CCTS and the EU's CBAM could prevent domestic compliance efforts from translating into meaningful deductions at the EU border.

While both the CCTS and CBAM target carbon emissions, their design principles and operational frameworks differ significantly. First, CBAM levies a price per tonne of emissions embedded in imports, whereas the CCTS is an intensity-based baseline-and-credit system in which sectors that outperform their targets earn CCCs and those that fall short face a statutory financial penalty. This architectural mismatch between India's CCTS and the EU's CBAM could prevent domestic compliance efforts from translating into meaningful deductions at the EU border.

Second, the CCTS is not recognised under Article 9 of the EU's CBAM regulation, which allows importers to reduce the number of CBAM certificates they must surrender by deducting any carbon price already paid in the country of origin. Although India secured a ‘forward-looking most-favoured-nation assurance’ under the FTA, under which flexibilities can be granted in implementation, this amounts to protection against discrimination rather than formal recognition.
Even if the EU were to recognise eligible and verifiable carbon costs incurred under the CCTS, the deduction would cover only a small fraction of India's CBAM liability.

Third, the price gap between the CCTS and CBAM is too wide to close. For instance, CCTS prices are currently estimated at roughly US$11-15 per tonne, while the CBAM certificate price stood at EUR 75.28 per tonne (or US$86.99 per tonne, at an exchange rate of EUR 1.00 = US$1.1555) in the second quarter of 2026. Even if the EU were to recognise eligible and verifiable carbon costs incurred under the CCTS, the deduction would cover only a small fraction of India's CBAM liability.

For India, CBAM brings carbon competitiveness to the forefront for sectors heavily dependent on exports to the EU, such as steel, aluminium, fertilisers, cement, metals, and mining. The additional carbon-related cost is unlikely to erode India's overall export competitiveness, but it could significantly affect the market position of individual firms and sectors. The challenge, therefore, is to find a middle ground in which the CCTS supports decarbonisation without adding to Indian exporters' cost pressures, while also facilitating compliance with CBAM.

The CCTS must develop stronger price discovery, supported by market liquidity, target stringency, and robust monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV), to generate a credible domestic carbon price. Greater EU clarity on eligible carbon costs, together with nationally consistent MRV requirements, is also necessary to reduce the compliance burden. Transition finance can complement the existing system by absorbing the abatement costs of decarbonisation. India could explore carbon-linked green bonds, particularly for CBAM-exposed sectors. By lowering the cost of financing cleaner technologies, such instruments would help firms cut emissions and, in turn, reduce future CCTS compliance costs and CBAM liabilities. Emissions-linked repayment terms could further incentivise firms to cut emissions.

Yet, CBAM embeds a long history of climate inequity with deeper structural asymmetries in global environmental governance. Shifting the burden of decarbonisation from the EU to developing economies threatens the prospect of a just transition.

One option is an India CBAM Levy Industrial Decarbonisation Fund. Under it, India would collect a levy on CBAM-covered exports and use the proceeds for industrial decarbonisation, while Brussels, in turn, would recognise this effort under Article 9 of the CBAM regulation.

India should consider two pathways to find a middle ground and offset the vulnerabilities that CBAM exposes. First, it could pursue diversification of exports away from the EU towards non-CBAM destinations such as Africa, Latin America, and the Middle East, which offer higher unit revenues. The additional revenue could, in effect, cover the cost of procuring CBAM certificates. A 2025 report by Ernst & Young (EY) argues that CBAM-induced diversification can work as a revenue-enhancing strategy rather than merely a defensive response.

Second, India could seek a two-way street of cooperation in which the EU supports India's decarbonisation journey. Given India's continued dependence on coal-based electricity generation and the significant variation in grid emissions intensity across states, exporters will eventually face substantially different CBAM costs depending on where they are located. While the CCTS may reduce part of India's CBAM exposure through convergence in domestic carbon pricing, it falls short of capturing the additional costs arising from regional differences in electricity grids. Decarbonising India's electricity sector is therefore equally critical to reducing long-term CBAM-related trade costs.

One option is an India CBAM Levy Industrial Decarbonisation Fund. Under it, India would collect a levy on CBAM-covered exports and use the proceeds for industrial decarbonisation, while Brussels, in turn, would recognise this effort under Article 9 of the CBAM regulation. Matching contributions from the EU would give it a co-governance role in setting the fund's objectives. A two-year pilot agreement, backed by the EU's new EUR 500 million climate finance commitment to India, could serve as a first test of the arrangement.

A supplementary element would involve small and medium enterprises (SMEs), which are among the worst hit by CBAM. Given their limited capacity to handle standardisation procedures and compliance demands, and their limited regulatory capacity and capital, Brussels should engage bilaterally to ensure that CBAM is treated not as a silver bullet for climate action or a tool for enhancing its own global competitiveness, but as a basis for collaborating with the Global South on long-term decarbonisation.
